prompt: In entities.py, why are the two members called Ana Souza not equal?

choices.text: Their phone numbers differ
choices.why: Both have +55 11 5550-0114; the program makes them identical on purpose.

choices.text: Their ids differ
choices.why: Right. m-014 and m-203 are two members whatever their attributes say.

choices.text: Python compares the two objects by their addresses in memory
choices.why: That is the default, and Member overrides it with __eq__.

prompt: entities.py puts ana, before and other_ana in a set. If Member had no __eq__ and __hash__ of its own, how many elements would the set hold?
hint: Without them, Python compares objects by identity in memory.

prompt: A team lets the database assign each member's id on INSERT. What problem does the section point out?

choices.text: Sequences run out after a few million rows
choices.why: Exhaustion is not the issue raised; timing is.

choices.text: Two members could end up with the same id
choices.why: A sequence does not repeat; the trouble is before it has been asked at all.

choices.text: Until it is saved, the member has no identity to compare or refer to
choices.why: Right. An entity needs its id from the moment it exists.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as every entity is saved immediately after it is made
choices.why: Even saved at once, it cannot go in a set or be named by another aggregate before the INSERT returns.

prompt: money.py prints True and then False for fine == Money(175) and fine is Money(175). Why is the False harmless?

choices.text: For a value, which object it is never matters
choices.why: Right. Equal values are interchangeable; only an entity cares about identity.

choices.text: It is a bug in the frozen dataclass that Python will fix
choices.why: is compares identity, and two separately made objects are two objects. Nothing is broken.

choices.text: Because the second Money has a different currency
choices.why: Both are BRL, the default; the == just above is True.

prompt: Why does the section give money a type instead of passing ints around?

choices.text: An int cannot hold amounts above a few million cents
choices.why: Python's int has no such limit; the reason is where the rules live.

choices.text: So money's rules live in one place
choices.why: Right. Currency mixing and half cents are refused once, in Money.

choices.text: Dataclasses make arithmetic faster than plain ints
choices.why: They make it slower, if anything; speed is not the point.

choices.text: Because a database column cannot store an integer amount
choices.why: SqliteMembers stores owed as an INTEGER without trouble.

prompt: Match each language to how it usually writes a value object.

pairs.right: a small struct passed by value
readonly fields plus an equals method

prompt: Why does Member.loans return a tuple rather than the list itself?

choices.text: Tuples use less memory, and members are loaded often
choices.why: Memory is not the reason; the tuple closes a door.

choices.text: So no code can add a loan except through borrow
choices.why: Right. A tuple has no append, so the five-loan rule cannot be bypassed that way.

choices.text: Because a dataclass cannot contain a list
choices.why: Member is not a dataclass, and dataclasses can hold lists.

prompt: A film is lent on 2 March 2026 and comes back on 20 March. Using member.py's rules, what fine is charged, in cents?
hint: A film goes out for 7 days.

prompt: A migration script needs to import old loans. It writes them straight into member._loans. What does the section's reasoning say about that?

choices.text: Fine, because migrations run only once
choices.why: Running once is enough to load a member with seven loans, and the root never sees it.

choices.text: It must go through the root, like every other path
choices.why: Right. Going through borrow, or a factory, is what keeps five loans the maximum.

choices.text: Python will raise an error because _loans is private
choices.why: The underscore is a convention; the write will succeed silently.

prompt: In copies.py, Bia is offered the extra copy while already holding five loans. What happens to the copy?

choices.text: It is never touched, because lend checks the member first
choices.why: lend changes the copy first and the member second.

choices.text: It stays out to Bia, and Caio is refused
choices.why: The transcript shows on loan to: None, and Caio gets it.

choices.text: It is checked out to her, then checked back in when she is refused
choices.why: Right. A correction made by code after the first change had already happened.

prompt: Copy.on_loan_to holds the member's ___ , a string such as m-002, and never the Member object.
A new rule: a member's holds and loans together may not exceed eight. Holds are their own aggregate. What does the section suggest asking first?

choices.text: Must it hold at every instant, or soon?
choices.why: Right. Most cross-boundary rules turn out to be "soon", and then an event and a handler will do.

choices.text: How to merge holds into the Member aggregate straight away
choices.why: That is one answer if the rule must hold at every instant, and it makes the aggregate bigger; ask first.

choices.text: Which of the two aggregates should hold a reference to the other object
choices.why: Aggregates refer to each other by id; holding the object is the second door.

prompt: Why is there a MemberRepository and no LoanRepository?

choices.text: Loans are stored in a file rather than the database
choices.why: Loans have a table of their own in SqliteMembers.

choices.text: Nobody has written it yet
choices.why: Its absence is deliberate, and the section argues for it.

choices.text: A loan never loads without its member
choices.why: Right. Repositories exist per aggregate root.

prompt: Why does InMemoryMembers keep deep copies instead of the members it is given?

choices.text: So a change counts only once it has been saved, as in a database
choices.why: Right. Otherwise a test would pass for code that forgot to call save.

choices.text: Deep copies make the tests run faster
choices.why: Copying is slower; the copies buy realism.

choices.text: Python dictionaries cannot hold objects that change later
choices.why: They can; that is exactly what would make the fake too forgiving.

choices.text: Because SqliteMembers does the same with its rows
choices.why: SQLite stores rows, not objects; the copies imitate that behaviour.

prompt: A teammate adds a method lend_directly(member_id, copy_id) to SqliteMembers that inserts a loan row. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: It is fine; it is faster than loading the member
choices.why: Faster, and it skips both of the member's rules.

choices.text: It changes the aggregate behind its root, skipping both limits
choices.why: Right. A repository gets and saves whole aggregates; it does not make business changes.

choices.text: It should be on InMemoryMembers too, so both classes match the protocol
choices.why: Adding it to both would put the second door in both places.

prompt: Why does Member record LoanStarted instead of sending the SMS receipt itself?

choices.text: The SMS gateway does not accept messages from objects
choices.why: The gateway is not the issue; the member's dependencies are.

choices.text: Events are faster to send than SMS messages
choices.why: The SMS is still sent, by a handler; speed does not change.

choices.text: The member says what happened; reactions belong elsewhere
choices.why: Right. Adding a reaction is a line in HANDLERS, and member.py does not change.

prompt: Put the steps of handlers.run in order.
items: Load the member from the repository
Ask the member to borrow or give back
Pull the events out of the member
Publish the events to the handlers
trap: Saving before pulling would store the events in the in-memory copy and hand them out again on the next get.

prompt: Publishing after saving can fail and leave a saved loan with no event sent. When does the section say that is not acceptable, and what does it offer?

choices.text: In any case; publish before saving instead
choices.why: Publishing first sends receipts for loans a failed save then loses.

choices.text: When another aggregate depends on it: write it to an outbox in the same transaction
choices.why: Right. A separate job publishes from the outbox and marks events sent.

choices.text: When the event is a receipt: retry the SMS three times
choices.why: A lost receipt is the case the section calls acceptable.

prompt: With FinePolicy and Carnaval closed on 16 and 17 February 2026, a book due on 15 February comes back on 18 February. What is the fine, in cents?
hint: Count the days after the due date the library was open.

prompt: Why does the closed-days rule get a FinePolicy of its own instead of a method on Loan?

choices.text: It needs the library's calendar, which no single loan or member should hold
choices.why: Right. A rule with no natural owner gets a home of its own.

choices.text: Services are always better than methods on entities
choices.why: That belief is the anaemic domain model the section warns against.

choices.text: Loan is a dataclass, and dataclasses cannot have methods
choices.why: Money is a dataclass with several methods.

prompt: Which of these are application services rather than domain services, in the section's terms? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: lend_copy in repositories.py
choices.why: Right. Load, ask, save: it coordinates and decides nothing.

choices.text: FinePolicy.fine_for in closures.py
choices.why: It decides something a librarian would recognise: a domain service.

choices.text: run in handlers.py
choices.why: Right. It loads, saves and publishes; every decision is the member's.

choices.text: Member.borrow in member.py
choices.why: That is a method of the aggregate root, not a service of either kind.

prompt: Match each piece of lending to the tactical pattern it is.
Acquisitions records "2 copies of ISBN 978-65-5555-001-6 at BRL 49.90". In lending, copy C-0107 is out to Bia. How should each be modelled?

choices.text: Both copies are entities everywhere, since a copy is a physical thing
choices.why: Physical or not, acquisitions cares about a quantity, not which copy is which.

choices.text: The desk's one is an entity; the order's 2 is only a value
choices.why: Right. The same concept is either, depending on the context.

choices.text: Both are values, because each has an ISBN that identifies it
choices.why: Two copies share one ISBN; C-0107 and C-0108 are not interchangeable at the desk.

prompt: Lending a copy changes the Copy and the Member. Which design follows both of the section's rules about boundaries?

choices.text: Put each Copy inside the Member who holds it, so one transaction covers both
choices.why: Then a copy has to be found inside whichever member holds it, and the aggregate grows without limit.

choices.text: Give Copy a reference to the Member object, so it can call borrow directly
choices.why: Holding the object is the second door; the rule is to refer by id.

choices.text: Own transactions, joined by ids, repaired by events
choices.why: Right. One aggregate per transaction, by id, and "soon" rather than "instant" between them.

choices.text: Lock both tables for the whole lend, every time
choices.why: That is the larger lock the section keeps for rules that must hold at every instant; lending is not one.
